title: AbbVie (ABBV) Stock Just Got a 5.2% Dividend Increase. Here's How Many Shares You Need to Generate $1,000 a Year. - The Globe and Mail
content: AbbVie's dividend yield of 2.4% is solid, but more importantly, it's been growing at an impressive clip. The stock isn't cheap, but it warrants consideration for a long-term portfolio. If you're in the market for a healthcare stock for your long-term portfolio, pharmaceutical giant AbbVie(NYSE:ABBV) offers several compelling reasons to invest in. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Here's a closer look at AbbVie and some of those reasons to consider it. First, though, let's talk dividends. AbbVie stock recently sported a dividend yield of 2.4%. That's quite solid, but it might have been higher had the stock not popped by 28% year to date (as of Nov. 18). (A stock's dividend yield is its total annual dividend amount divided by the stock price, so when the stock price rises, the yield falls, and vice versa.) Better still, it's a growing dividend. The current $1.82 quarterly payout is up 5.2% from the previous $1.73, and up from $1.41 in 2022 and $0.57 in 2016. And AbbVie has hiked its payout for 53 years in a row, making it a Dividend King. Let's say you're looking for $1,000 in annual income from AbbVie. How many shares would you need to own? The math is straightforward: The total payout for the year is $1.82 times four, or $7.28 for the year. Divide $1,000 by $7.28, and you'll get the needed number of shares: 137.36. At a recent stock price of $284 per share, 137 shares will cost you... roughly $39,000. But would you want to invest in AbbVie? I'm a shareholder myself, but I'd hesitate to jump in right now because the recent valuation seems a bit high. The recent price-to-sales ratio of 7.7, for example, is well above the five-year average of 5.4, and the forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 17.6 is also well above the five-year average of 13.9. So maybe just add it to your watch list, hoping for a lower entry point. Or just start a small position in it now -- as long as you aim to hang on for many years. Its last earnings report was good, with revenue up 10% year over year and immunology drugs Skyrizi and Rinvoq performing particularly well. title: Abbott Laboratories (NYSE: ABT), AbbVie (NYSE: ABBV), And Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO) Stand Out As Elite Dividend Compounders Built To Last - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 19, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Abbott Laboratories (NYSE: ABT) made headlines this year after closing a $21 billion cash deal to acquire Exact Sciences, a company focused on cancer diagnostics. The acquisition targets one of Abbott’s slower-growing business units and signals a strategic push to strengthen its diagnostic capabilities in an increasingly competitive healthcare market. Abbott also leads the continuous glucose monitoring space through its FreeStyle Libre franchise, giving it a meaningful foothold in one of medical technology’s fastest-expanding categories. Despite a stretch of mediocre financial results and lingering legal and regulatory headaches, the company’s dividend growth streak remains intact, and analysts see little reason to expect that to change anytime soon. AbbVie (NYSE: ABBV), which was carved out of Abbott as a standalone public company in 2013, has built a compelling track record of its own since then, outperforming the broader market across that span. The pharmaceutical company’s two flagship immunology drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, have consistently exceeded expectations and face no U.S. patent expiration until at least 2033. That long runway gives AbbVie unusual earnings visibility for a large-cap drugmaker, along with time to develop new medicines that could sustain growth well beyond the current decade. AbbVie has demonstrated an ability to navigate patent cliffs without sacrificing dividend momentum, and the company has now raised its payout for 64 consecutive years when counting the time it operated under Abbott’s umbrella. Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO) rounds out the group with a similarly long dividend streak of 64 consecutive years, a figure that places it among the most consistent income generators in the entire equity market. The beverage giant has continued to deliver stability and a reliable income program even as consumers globally have faced persistent cost-of-living pressures and an uncertain macroeconomic backdrop. All three companies belong to the Dividend Kings, a designation reserved for corporations that have raised their dividends for at least 50 straight years, an elite threshold that fewer than a handful of businesses ever reach. What separates these three from the broader Dividend Kings universe is a combination of operational depth, market leadership, and the kind of structural advantages that tend to compound investor returns over very long holding periods.
